summary: Describes Magma, the 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key defined in the Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015, alongside the 128-bit cipher Kuznyechik covered in RFC 7801. It is published to help implementers and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A cipher is a recipe for scrambling messages. Magma is one such recipe from a Russian national standard. This document writes it down so programmers outside the original standard can build it the same way.

questions: how many rounds does magma have
subtitle: An English description of Magma, the 64-bit block cipher with a 256-bit key from a Russian national standard.

tldr.problem: The Russian standard GOST R 34.12-2015 updated an older 64-bit block cipher, and implementers outside the standard's origin needed an English description of it.
tldr.mechanism: Magma encrypts a 64-bit block with a 256-bit key in 32 rounds. Each round substitutes 4-bit pieces through eight S-boxes, rotates left by 11 bits and mixes the result into the other half of the block with exclusive-or.
tldr.outcome: The document is informational and updates RFC 5830. It gives test vectors but defines no block modes, so protocols pick their own.

today: RFC 8891 is an Informational RFC published in September 2020. It updates RFC 5830 and has not been obsoleted or updated itself.

sections.title: What Magma Is
sections.content:
RFC 8891 describes Magma, the block cipher with a block length of 64 bits and a key length of 256 bits that is part of the Russian Federal standard GOST R 34.12-2015. The standard's other cipher, the 128-bit Kuznyechik, is covered in RFC 7801.

The standard was developed by the Center for Information Protection and Special Communications of the Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation. It was approved by Decree #749 on June 19, 2015. The algorithms are designed for both hardware and software implementation.

The RFC is an Independent Submission, not a standard. It exists to give developers and users information about the revised cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: Magma is a secret-code machine with a 64-bit mailbox size and a very long key. This document explains how to build it.

sections.title: How Magma Relates to GOST 28147-89
sections.content:
Magma is an updated version of the older 64-bit cipher in GOST 28147-89, which RFC 5830 describes. Appendix B lists the differences:

  • The S-box set is fixed at id-tc26-gost-28147-param-Z.
  • The key is parsed as a single big-endian integer, where the old cipher used little-endian, so different subkey values result.
  • Data bytes are also parsed as a single big-endian integer.

The RFC also calls itself a translation of relevant parts of the standard. Together with RFC 7801 it forms a complete English translation of GOST R 34.12-2015.
sections.plainLanguage: Magma is a fixed-up version of an older recipe. The main change is which end of a number gets read first.

sections.title: S-Boxes and Round Transformations
sections.content:
The nonlinear part is a set of eight substitutions, Pi_0 to Pi_7, each mapping a 4-bit value to another 4-bit value. Each is a bijection, so it can be undone.

Four transformations build the cipher, all working on 32-bit halves of the block:

  • t splits a 32-bit value into eight 4-bit pieces and runs piece i through Pi_i.
  • g[k] adds the round key k modulo 2^32, applies t, then rotates the result left by 11 bits.
  • G[k] takes the pair (a_1, a_0) and returns (a_0, g[k](a_0) xor a_1). This is one round.
  • G*[k] is the final round. It returns the 64-bit value (g[k](a_0) xor a_1) || a_0, so the halves are not swapped.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight secret lookup tables swap small numbers for other numbers. Each round then looks things up, spins the bits and stirs them into the other half of the message.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The 256-bit key K is cut into eight 32-bit words, K_1 to K_8, starting from the most significant bits. The 32 round keys are then made like this:

  • K_9 to K_16 repeat K_1 to K_8.
  • K_17 to K_24 repeat them again.
  • K_25 to K_32 use them in reverse order, so K_25 is K_8 and K_32 is K_1.
sections.plainLanguage: The long key is cut into eight pieces. The pieces are used in order three times, then once backwards.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
Encryption applies G[K_1] through G[K_31] in turn to the two halves of the 64-bit block, then finishes with G*[K_32]. That is 32 rounds in total.

Decryption uses the same structure with the round keys in the opposite order: G[K_32] down to G[K_2], then G*[K_1].

Appendix A gives test vectors. With the key ffeeddccbbaa99887766554433221100f0f1f2f3f4f5f6f7f8f9fafbfcfdfeff, the plaintext fedcba9876543210 encrypts to 4ee901e5c2d8ca3d, and decrypting that gives the plaintext back.
sections.plainLanguage: To lock a message you run the same stirring 32 times. To unlock it you run the same steps with the key pieces in reverse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that the entire document is about security considerations. Unlike RFC 5830, but like RFC 7801, it does not define block modes to use with Magma. Implementers are free to choose modes to suit the protocol.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe only scrambles one small block. You choose for yourself how to handle long messages.
